questions.question: How would you design an A/B test for a new feature?
expected_key_points: State a falsifiable hypothesis linking the feature to a primary metric before launch
Randomize at the user level with stable IDs and sticky bucketing
Pick one primary metric plus guardrails; pre-commit runtime via power analysis
Validate with an SRM check before reading any metric

questions.question: How long should an experiment run?
expected_key_points: Run a power analysis: choose MDE from business relevance (1-2% for mature products)
Sample size scales as variance over MDE squared
Cover full weekly cycles and pre-commit the runtime; do not extend on a whim

questions.question: Why shouldn't you stop a test the moment the p-value first falls below 0.05?
expected_key_points: Repeated interim testing inflates the Type I error rate well above the nominal 5%
A p-value is only valid for a pre-committed sample size and analysis plan
Fix with pre-committed runtime, sequential methods, or alpha spending

questions.question: How would you choose a primary success metric for an experiment?
expected_key_points: The metric must be aligned with the hypothesis and the business goal
It must be sensitive enough to move with the treatment (consider variance/MDE)
Pair it with guardrail metrics for trade-offs; one primary avoids multiplicity

questions.question: Conversion improves significantly but retention declines. Do you ship?
expected_key_points: No automatic ship: the launch rule is conjunctive, guardrails can veto
Quantify the trade-off rather than eyeballing it
Veto thresholds should have been pre-committed before readout

questions.question: How would you detect sample ratio mismatch?
expected_key_points: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test of observed arm counts against the designed ratio
Investigate before reading any metric; SRM is a smoke alarm for broken randomization
Enumerate root causes: bucketing bugs, bots, triggered-analysis joins, overlapping launches

questions.question: What if users switch between treatment and control — for example through shared devices?
expected_key_points: This is contamination and it attenuates the estimated effect toward zero
Detect it with exposure logging of treatment-only events in control
Prevent with stable-ID randomization and sticky bucketing

questions.question: What if the treatment affects users who were not assigned to it?
expected_key_points: This violates SUTVA — it is interference/spillover, and naive estimates mix direct and spillover effects
Diagnose with cluster-robust vs naive standard errors
Design fix: cluster randomization at the level where SUTVA plausibly holds

questions.question: What if the treatment effect varies by customer segment?
expected_key_points: Heterogeneity is real but segment-hunting is multiple testing: ~1 false positive per 20 cuts at 0.05
Correct with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR; pre-register segments before readout
A credible HTE claim needs FDR survival plus a plausible mechanism

questions.question: Your experiment comes back statistically insignificant. What do you do?
expected_key_points: Read the confidence interval, not just the p-value: a wide CI means 'we don't know', not 'no effect'
Check whether the experiment was powered for a realistic MDE
Decide among: extend on a pre-committed plan, iterate on the treatment, or kill it

questions.question: DashPass subscribers order more than non-subscribers. Does DashPass cause higher ordering?
expected_key_points: No — this is selection bias: subscribers were already heavier users
Compare against matched non-subscribers with similar observables and show balance tables
Matching cannot fix selection on unobservables; an experiment is the gold standard

questions.question: How would you estimate the impact of a feature launched in only some markets?
expected_key_points: Use difference-in-differences: compare the change in treated markets to the change in control markets
The identifying assumption is parallel trends — validate with pre-period placebo tests
Watch for spillover between markets and compositional change

questions.question: How would you compare feature adopters against non-adopters who have different baseline characteristics?
expected_key_points: Match on pre-treatment observables, e.g. via propensity scores
Demonstrate balance with balance tables after matching
The approach assumes selection on observables; unmeasured confounding remains a threat

questions.question: How would you evaluate a program that is assigned using an eligibility threshold, like a risk-score cutoff?
expected_key_points: Use a regression discontinuity design: compare units just above vs just below the cutoff
Check for manipulation of the running variable with density/bunching tests at the cutoff
The effect is local to the cutoff and need not generalize far away

questions.question: Did a product change alter the trend after launch, in a single market with no control group?
expected_key_points: Use interrupted time series: project the pre-launch trend forward and compare to observed post data
Requires a long, stable pre-period; concurrent changes are the main confounder
Without a control group the conclusion is suggestive, not causal — say so

questions.question: How can pre-experiment behavior reduce the variance of an experiment?
expected_key_points: CUPED: regress the metric on pre-period covariates and analyze the residuals
Typical ~50% variance reduction is equivalent to doubling the sample size
Covariates must be pre-treatment; the method fails on whale-dominated metrics and new users

questions.question: You cut results by 20 segments and several come back significant. How do you interpret them?
expected_key_points: Expect roughly one false positive per 20 cuts at alpha = 0.05 by chance alone
Apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control before believing any segment
Trust pre-registered segments over data-mined ones; demand a mechanism

questions.question: Overall conversion increased, yet every major segment declined. Explain.
expected_key_points: This is Simpson's paradox, driven by a mix/composition shift toward a high-converting segment
Inspect segment composition alongside the topline number
Decide whether the business cares about the marginal or the conditional effect

questions.question: How do you calculate uncertainty for a ratio metric like orders per active customer?
expected_key_points: Use the delta method or bootstrap for standard errors; naive per-user averaging mishandles zero denominators
Check for denominator shifts: treatment changing who is active can move the ratio spuriously
Analyze numerator and denominator separately when the denominator is affected

questions.question: How should a marketplace experiment handle geographic spillovers between arms?
expected_key_points: Randomize at the market/geography level — cluster randomization keeps spillover inside the cluster
Effective sample size is the number of clusters, so power depends on cluster count
Analyze with cluster-robust standard errors

questions.question: The peeker's mirage: early enrollees showed +3.8% (p=2.7e-09), but the full sample shows +0.15% (p=0.647). Should we ship?
expected_key_points: No — the interim significance without sequential correction is peeking, and the p-value is invalid
The full-sample result (+0.15%, p=0.647) is the valid readout: inconclusive
Interim looks are diagnostic, never decisive

questions.question: Whale variance: revenue per user is up about 36% and statistically significant, but the between-arm std ratio is roughly 3.0. Is the lift real?
expected_key_points: Do not trust it: a std ratio near 3.0 with a headline lift is the whale signature
A few extreme users are manufacturing the mean lift; check medians and winsorized means
The honest verdict is inconclusive — the experiment cannot separate real lift from whale luck

questions.question: Dilution trap: ITT is +0.35% (p=0.27) but CACE is +2.10% (p=0.0004) at a 30% trigger rate. What happened, and which number matters?
expected_key_points: The low trigger rate diluted the true effect: ITT is roughly trigger-rate times CACE
CACE answers whether the feature works; ITT answers the business impact of launching
Report both, and do not call the experiment a failure from the ITT alone

questions.question: Trigger imbalance: the naive triggered estimate is -2.1% but the true effect is +2.0%. Why did the sign flip?
expected_key_points: Trigger rates differ by arm, so the triggered subset is self-selected: selection bias
The balance check on trigger rates is the gate that should have caught this
CUPED only partially debiases selection on observables; the verdict is inconclusive

questions.question: Guardrail veto: engagement is up significantly, but the user-reports rate rose about 28%. Launch?
expected_key_points: Do not launch: the guardrail veto is conjunctive with the primary win
A large guardrail movement blocks launch even if the primary metric is significant
Veto thresholds should have been pre-committed before readout
